newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Asia Metals - Aluminium premiums jump, zinc slumps.
newsitem.headline: Asia Metals - Aluminium premiums jump, zinc slumps.

text.p: Aluminium premiums in Singapore soared due to a severe shortage of the metal while zinc premiums slipped further due to abundant supplies in warehouses here, base metal dealers said on Friday.

Premiums for western aluminium 20-25 kg ingots rose to US$80-$100 a tonne from $55-$75 at the beginning of June while Indian aluminium 20-25 kg ingots shot up to $65-$75 from $40-$60 last month, the dealers said.
"We are sold out. We have nothing to sell in Singapore," a senior dealer for a major metal trading company told Reuters. "It's very tight. No one can make you an offer at the moment."
"Aluminium is very tight right now," a veteran Japanese dealer said. "It's very difficult to get any supply."
Premiums have shot up as a result of low stocks in the warehouse of the London Metal Exchange (LME) in Singapore.
The volume of aluminium stocks at the LME's warehouse in the city-state reached 6,625 tonnes on Thursday, down almost two-thirds of the 15,825 tonnes reported at the end of April.
"That's why the premiums are up. The stocks here are half of what they were two months ago," one dealer said.
Robust regional demand has also underpinned the strong aluminium premiums.
Spot premiums in Japan touched $98 a tonne CIF Japanese ports compared to premiums of around $90-$93 a few weeks ago.

"Many consumers in Malaysia take it for granted they can get material from Singapore. But I don't think they will be able to do so now," a dealer said. "There's no sign that regional demand is weakening."
Aluminium dealers said supplies of Indian aluminium have been particularly scarce.
"Very little Indian material is coming in. I think NALCO (National Aluminium Co) is a little bit behind in their deliveries," one dealer said.
Traders estimate that the volume of aluminium shipments from NALCO had declined further to less than 200 tonnes a month from the normal average of 500-800 tonnes.
The situation is sharply different in zinc, where the arrival of large supplies from China has sent premiums in Singapore crashing.
Premiums for 25-kg zinc ingots slumped to $1-$5 a tonne, down from last week's $3-$5 and the level a few months ago of $20-$30, dealers said.
"Those premiums are already at the bottom. I don't see how much lower they can go," a dealer said.
The premiums have collapsed largely as a result of a buildup in zinc stocks at the LME's Singapore warehouse.
The volume of zinc here reached 34,375 tonnes on Thursday against 12,700 tonnes at the beginning of May.
Traders believe about 10,000 tonnes of zinc remain off-warrant and that another 5,000-10,000 tonnes of zinc from China is on the way here.
"I think 10,000 tonnes is still off-warrant and there are a lot of rumours that 10,000 tonnes from China is on the way here," a zinc dealer said.
"I don't know how much more the Chinese can afford to ship. There's so much material here already," another dealer said.
Traders said zinc is being stored in Singapore warehouses because of the strong rally in zinc prices on the LME, where the metal is seen testing a fresh high of $1,500 a tonne later on Friday.
-- Singapore Newsroom (65-8703305)
